title: 350,000 Haitians Face Deportation as Court Lifts Final TPS Protection
excerpt: A federal judge confirmed the end of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, triggering ICE enforcement operations and sending shockwaves through the elder care industry.
body:
• A federal judge officially ended TPS protections for roughly 350,000 Haitians, clearing the way for deportation to a country the State Department has repeatedly warned is dangerous and unstable.
  • ICE has already begun targeting former TPS holders, fitting some with ankle monitors, as DHS pledges aggressive enforcement.
  • The Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling in June stripped courts of authority to review TPS termination decisions, potentially affecting 1.3 million immigrants from 17 countries.
  • Nearly 190,000 Haitian TPS holders were employed in the U.S., contributing an estimated $5.9 billion to the economy, with the elder care industry facing the most immediate disruption.

Court Ends Months of Legal Uncertainty

A federal judge on August 5 officially confirmed that temporary deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians are no longer in effect, marking the final legal step in a months-long battle that reached the Supreme Court and now clears the path for one of the largest immigration enforcement campaigns in recent U.S. history.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes lifted the stay that had paused the Department of Homeland Security's termination of Haiti's Temporary Protected Status designation. The order ends weeks of confusion among the roughly 350,000 Haitians who had benefited from the program, which allowed them to live and work legally in the United States after fleeing political unrest and natural disasters.

"As a result of today's order implementing the Supreme Court's decision, Haitian TPS holders — all of them non-criminals — can no longer legally work, and many are subject to removal to Haiti, which continues to be one of the most dangerous countries in the world," said Geoff Pipoly, an attorney representing the Haitian plaintiffs.

Supreme Court Set the Stage in June

The order follows the Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling on June 25, which overturned lower court decisions blocking the Trump administration from ending TPS for Haitians and Syrians. Conservative Justice Samuel Alito, writing for the majority, held that federal courts cannot review the administration's decisions to terminate TPS designations — a finding that could doom legal challenges for immigrants from any of the 17 countries currently covered by the program.

"The references — of filth, disease and primitiveness — are shot through with racial stereotypes and tropes. It is hard to imagine the statements being made today of any White community."

— Justice Elena Kagan, Supreme Court dissent

Justice Elena Kagan, writing in dissent, pointed to Trump's false claims during the 2024 campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio were eating pets, calling the rhetoric rooted in racial stereotypes. Alito dismissed the racial animus argument, writing that the evidence showed a "strong, race-neutral explanation" — that the administration simply opposes the TPS program as it has been implemented.

ICE Begins Enforcement Operations

Immigration and Customs Enforcement had already started targeting TPS holders before the August 5 order, according to CNN, with some Haitians called into ICE offices and fitted with ankle monitors. DHS Secretary Markwaye Mullin was blunt about the government's intentions.

"We're going after them right now," Mullin told NewsNation. "These individuals can either self-deport or we'll arrest you and send you back. It's that simple."

Some former TPS holders who were pursuing other forms of immigration relief, such as asylum claims, may not be immediately affected. But for the vast majority, the protections that allowed them to build lives in the United States over more than a decade are gone.

Elder Care Industry Faces Immediate Worker Shortages

The economic fallout is already visible. Westminster Communities of Florida terminated 12 Haitian TPS holders who worked as certified nursing assistants, dining services staff, and housekeepers, replacing them with temporary workers. The disruption extends to residents who had built relationships with their caregivers over years, according to the facility's chief human resources officer.

Nearly 190,000 Haitian TPS holders were employed in early 2025, contributing an estimated $5.9 billion to the U.S. economy and paying $1.6 billion in federal, payroll, state, and local taxes, according to an analysis by FWD.us. The elder care, hospitality, retail, and restaurant sectors face the most immediate workforce losses.

Republican Governor Mike DeWine of Ohio called the Supreme Court ruling "a mistake" that would hurt the state's economy. More than 10,000 Haitians had been living and working legally in the Springfield area through TPS, revitalizing communities that had struggled with population decline.

What Comes Next

The underlying legal case continues, with Haitian plaintiffs pressing their claim that the administration acted with discriminatory intent when it terminated TPS. Attorneys plan to marshal additional evidence to strengthen the equal protection argument that the Supreme Court found insufficient in its June ruling.

Meanwhile, judges in separate cases involving TPS holders from Ethiopia, Burma, and South Sudan have blocked enforcement on new legal grounds, sparking backlash from the administration. In Congress, a House vote in April to extend TPS for Haiti passed 224-204 with bipartisan support, but without Senate action the legislative effort has stalled.

"Immigrants are one of America's greatest strengths. The responsibility to save these lives is now with Congress."

— Geoff Pipoly and Andy Tauber, attorneys for Haitian TPS holders

The ruling carries implications well beyond Haiti. The Supreme Court's finding that courts cannot review TPS termination decisions affects approximately 1.3 million immigrants from 17 countries. For immigration attorneys and advocates, the decision fundamentally reshapes the legal landscape for temporary protections that many had treated as semi-permanent fixtures of the U.S. immigration system.
nri_angle: The Supreme Court ruling that courts cannot review TPS terminations sets a sweeping precedent affecting 1.3 million immigrants from 17 countries, fundamentally reshaping the legal landscape for all temporary immigration protections in the United States.
author: Diaspora Desk
